title: The farewell sermon
hookLine: lives and property sacred, women treated kindly, no Arab above non-Arab except by goodness

cards: If you had one last chance to talk to everyone who mattered to you, all at once, what would you say? Not the small stuff: the things you'd want them to hold on to after you were gone.
On the plain of Arafah, during that one Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ sat on his camel and spoke.
The crowd was so huge that, the biographers say, a man with a strong voice repeated his words outward, sentence by sentence, like ripples.
Muslims call it the farewell sermon, and different parts of it are preserved in different hadith collections.

teach.h: A PERSON IS AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.
teach.b: First: your lives and your property are sacred to one another, as sacred as this day, in this month, in this city. He took the holiest time and place they knew and said: a person is that holy.

teach.h: HE CANCELED HIS OWN FAMILY'S CLAIMS FIRST.
teach.b: Then he canceled the old blood feuds of the days before Islam, and the old debts of interest, and he began with his own family's claims. You can't ask others to drop their grudges if you keep yours.
Then: fear God concerning women. He reminded the men that they had taken their wives on a trust from God, and that the women had rights over them, including to be provided for with kindness.

And there's a line from a sermon during that pilgrimage, preserved in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad: no Arab has any superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a white person over a Black person, nor a Black person over a white person, except by goodness, by taqwa, mindfulness of God.

It echoes a verse of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." To know one another, not to rank one another.
He told them he was leaving them the Book of God. Then he asked the crowd: have I conveyed it to you? They said yes.
And he lifted his finger to the sky, pointed it toward the people, and said: O God, bear witness.

how: Muslims read and teach the farewell sermon, often in the days of Hajj and in Friday sermons, as a summary of the Prophet's message on the sacredness of life, the rights of women and the equality of people.

o: mindfulness of God in how you live
strict, exact keeping of every rule
a night prayer said in a mosque

games.q: what the sermon said — tap the pairs.
p: that ye may know one another

s: the whole sermon is preserved in one hadith
different parts of it are preserved in different collections.
he began canceling old claims with his own family's
the feuds and interest debts of his own relatives went first.
the sermon ranks people by their tribe
no Arab above a non-Arab, nor white above Black, except by goodness.

games.q: you're canceling the old blood feuds and interest debts in front of the whole crowd. whose do you cancel first?
o: your enemies' tribes, to show them mercy.
games.why: he began with his own family's claims. you can't ask others to drop their grudges if you keep yours.

practice: Think of someone you tend to rank, even silently: above you, a boss, someone richer or cleverer; or below you, someone younger, poorer, newer, from somewhere you've judged.
Picture them standing beside you on that plain, same height, same cloth, and hold them there, level, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask to see people as the sermon did.

wordCard.voice: Taqwa. Mindfulness of God — the one measure the Prophet gave for superiority among people, in his farewell sermon on the plain of Arafah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the farewell sermon. khutbah is a sermon; wada' is farewell.

carryVoice: Your line: no one above another. Only goodness weighs, nothing else. That's day two hundred eighty-five.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (a man repeats the Prophet's words to the crowd at Arafah)

sources.q: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1218 (the sermon at Arafah: lives and property sacred; feuds and interest canceled; fear God concerning women; the Book of God; O God, bear witness)
Musnad Ahmad 23489 (no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab except by taqwa)
